headlines.title: Disabled train prompts major BART delay
headlines.description: A disabled train between the Fremont and Union City stations is causing major delays on the Berryessa line, according to BART. Initially, BART had said the delay was 20 minutes. This is a developing story. This story uses functionality that may not work in our app. Click here to open the story in your web browser.

headlines.title: UC Berkeley student says she was followed, chased into her apartment complex
headlines.description: A UC Berkeley student said she was followed and chased into her off-campus apartment building on Tuesday night. Berkeley junior Eden Winograd said this all happened at around 8 p.m. on Tuesday when she was walking her dog near her off-campus apartment complex. That night, Winograd said she was walking her dog on the same path she does every night when she noticed a man approaching whom she had seen a few days earlier. “I started to panic a little bit, but I didn’t want to offend him if he was just standing there,” she said, recalling that she then started crossing the street. But then, she said the man started following directly behind her and saying things to her while she walked. “I started speeding up and heard his feet banging on the floor behind me,” she said. “I went up to the gate, I buzzed myself in, I went, and I closed it, and then I heard clanging sounds while I was walking inside, and I turned around, and he was like scaling the gate,” Winograd continued. “My heart sank, I was out of breath, my heart was pounding,” she recalled. She made it inside the elevator of her building before anything else happened, then called the police. Winograd posted the surveillance video of the incident on TikTok, where it has now been viewed more than 858,000 times. That surveillance video has now also been shared by Berkeley Police. The video shows Winograd walking into the gate of her apartment complex, walking her dog on a leash. A few seconds later, a man can be seen climbing over the same gate where she entered and following in the same direction Winograd walked in, holding something in his hand. Police said that initial reports indicated the suspect had a knife in his hand, but investigators later found that the object was likely a barbecue lighter. It is still unclear why that man would be holding a barbecue lighter. But for Winograd, that doesn’t change how alarming this incident was. “I don’t care if they have a weapon in their hand or nothing in their hand, I don’t want to be chased the second I step out of my apartment. I don’t want to be chased and have to watch someone claw their way up a wall to get to where I live,” she said. Police said that the following day, they were called about the same man lying on the sidewalk in the same area. Berkeley police said they detained him and confirmed he was involved in “the prior trespassing incident.” Police did not arrest that man, but they did send a case to the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office for review. Police have not released the man’s name, but they said he is 50 years old and experiencing homelessness.

headlines.title: Surveillance video shows moment ICE agent's gun found in San Francisco airport bathroom
headlines.description: Surveillance video from San Francisco International Airport obtained by NBC Bay Area is shedding more light on a July incident where an ICE deportation officer allegedly left his gun unattended in an airport restroom. A review of roughly two hours of CCTV footage – obtained through a California Public Records Act request – shows the moment the gun was found inside a bathroom stall by a flight attendant, along with the likely moment the ICE agent returned to the scene roughly 10 minutes later. As NBC Bay Area first reported in August, the firearm was found unattended inside a bathroom stall past security checkpoint D in Terminal 2, according to airport spokesperson Doug Yakel. Around 10:23 p.m., the surveillance video shows a person who appears to be the flight attendant run out of the bathroom and flag down airport security. The flight attendant and security officer then head back to the bathroom. Airport security then calls 9-1-1 and reports the gun to San Francisco police. “Hi, yeah, a flight attendant just came up to me and said there is a gun in the men’s bathroom,” an airport security officer tells police in a recording of the 9-1-1 call. San Francisco Aug 26 San Francisco Aug 27 The video shows additional law enforcement officers quickly arrive to investigate. Multiple travelers are turned away from the bathroom by police or security. The video makes it clear that dozens of people could potentially have found the gun if the flight attendant had not spotted it and notified security. Roughly 10 minutes after the flight attendant appears to discover the gun, the surveillance video shows a man dressed in plain clothes approach security outside the bathroom, present what looks like a badge, and enter the bathroom. The airport confirmed the man seen in the video was the ICE agent returning for his firearm. The video shows the apparent ICE agent emerge from the bathroom more than 10 minutes later with other law enforcement officials. He remains in front of the bathroom, where he seems to talk to officers on scene and present some sort of identification. Officers soon verify the gun belongs to the agent, according to police radio traffic. “We verified his firearm serial number through the government website,” someone says in the recording. Due to the position of the video camera and the quality of the video, it was not immediately clear to NBC Bay Area when the agent may have first left the gun in the bathroom. For weeks, NBC Bay Area has been asking ICE if the agent has faced any discipline for misplacing his gun, but the agency has not responded.
headlines.source: Hilda Gutierrez, Michael Bott and Alex Bozovic

headlines.title: Mountain lion released back into the wild after being captured in San Francisco
headlines.description: A young mountain lion was released back into the wild Friday after it was safely captured in San Francisco’s Sunset District. The mountain lion in the morning was spotted in yards and on a street. Video also showed the mountain lion on 44th Avenue. Neighbors said the animal moved from one bush to another in front of homes and stayed there. Police, animal control and other agencies responded. The street was blocked off and neighbors were told to stay back as officials worked to tranquilize the mountain lion. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife said the mountain lion was darted and ran off before the tranquilizer took effect. Officials then performed a quick health assessment and determined the animal was a male between 2 and 3 years old and weighed roughly 78 pounds. It was a morning that neighbors won’t soon forget. “It ran right in front of our house, and then they tranquilized it, and we saw it run out into the street too,” San Francisco resident Alex Grant said. “It was wild to see a mountain lion in a big city like this. It’s pretty incredible,” Grant added. Another neighbor, Carson Ryan, said he came to the area after seeing the police response. “I made my way over here at 10 o’clock. That’s when I saw all the police cars, caution tape, and I hung around and wanted to see what was really a mountain lion in the Outer Sunset, which it was,” Ryan said. After the mountain lion was safely captured, Fish and Wildlife officials placed a tracking collar on it and returned it to the wild. Officials said they are not sure where the mountain lion came from, but it could have traveled from the Peninsula, where there is habitat. headlines.title: San Francisco security guards strike to demand better pay and benefits
headlines.description: Security guards across California are demanding higher wages and better benefits. On Friday, several hundred security guards held a one-day strike in San Francisco. San Francisco security guard Jakia Lane says she goes to work every day not knowing what danger she may face. “They want us to protect them, but they don’t want to protect us,” she said. “It is in the back of my mind, but I also try to keep situational awareness, so that I’m aware because you never know what somebody’s gonna do to you. These people can stab you, shoot you, walk up to you and shoot you, anything.” Lane and her fellow security guards say they don’t earn a living wage. Security guards staged a one-day strike in San Francisco today to demand better pay and benefits from the companies that employ them. “Right now, we’re looking at average pay between $22 and $23 an hour and we really think those are wages that are not going to be able to sustain families,” SEIU Union President David Huerta said. Huerta says guards deserve at least $30 an hour, better health and retirement benefits, and better training. But contract negotiations with their employers have stalled. The union has been negotiating with security contractors including Allied Universal, Securitas, GardaWorld and others for months. NBC Bay Area reached out to the security contractors and heard back from just one of them. Allied Universal says they’re focused on reaching an agreement saying, “We have made substantial progress in negotiations as part of our commitment to finding common ground.” Meanwhile, Lane says she’s juggling her guard duties with a second job as a hair stylist just to survive. She says she and her colleagues deserve better. The union says contract talks will resume on Tuesday. But they say if a deal isn’t reached, the picketing that took place in San Francisco could become widespread. “We could see strikes as early as next week in Los Angeles some of the biggest economic corridors, we could see strikes in the Silicon Valley. We could see strikes in the east Bay and most certainly here in San Francisco,” Huerta said.

headlines.title: Police investigate deadly shooting in Oakland
headlines.description: A man died following a shooting in Oakland on Friday, according to the police department. Police said the incident occurred shortly before 6 p.m. in the 1500 block of Magnolia Street. Authorities said they found a man with an apparent gunshot wound, who died at the scene. The police department said a suspect was arrested in connection with the incident, and the department’s Homicide Section is conducting a follow-up investigation into the circumstances surrounding the man’s death.

headlines.description: Oakland is testing out a program aimed at cleaning up city streets, while helping unhoused people who participate get off the streets. Velena Jones has more in the video above. headlines.title: The Bernal Scream haunted house returns to San Jose
headlines.description: The Bernal Scream haunted house returned to San Jose Friday, and it’s bigger than ever. The homegrown haunt has nearly doubled its footprint this year to nearly 10,000 square feet. For the first time, it includes two main attractions: The Last Confession and Anxiety. The Last Confession takes visitors on a harrowing journey through their darkest sins. Anxiety is a psychological gauntlet designed to trigger primal phobias. The event also includes bouncy houses for younger children and glow-in-the-dark paintball. It opened its doors at 7:15 p.m. Friday and runs through Nov. 8.

headlines.title: CHP Solano catches driver sleeping inside Tesla going 60 mph
headlines.description: Solano CHP said Friday it caught a driver sleeping in his Tesla while going 60 miles an hour. The CHP says the driver thought he could hide the fact he was asleep behind dark sunglasses, but an officer spotted the driver slumping over. The CHP reminds everyone that self-driving features are meant to help but not replace drivers.

headlines.title: Humpback whale spotted swimming in Sacramento River
headlines.description: A humpback whale has been spotted swimming in the California Delta, with new video capturing the animal near the Rio Vista Bridge. The whale was originally spotted Tuesday near the Richmond shipping channel. On Wednesday afternoon, a man fishing near the Rio Vista Bridge in Rio Vista captured video of the whale. He said he initially thought his friend was mistaken about seeing it. The Delta is no stranger to whales. In 1985, a whale named Humphrey spent several weeks in the Rio Vista area before eventually returning to the ocean. In 2007, a mother whale and her calf also spent several weeks in the Delta. Scientists are asking people to keep their distance from the whale.

headlines.title: Laws ban surprise medical bills. But you might still get one if you call 911
headlines.description: One woman’s medical emergency might open your eyes to a costly “gap” in health coverage. “I probably would have died if the ambulance did not show up,” said Sophia, who asked NBC Bay Area not to use her last name. She was walking with a friend last year when she suddenly felt sick. “My friend called 911,” Sophia said. NBC Bay Area obtained a recording of the 911 call. “She’s cold as ice… She’s drooling,” the caller said. An operator asked, “Is she responding normally?” Hurriedly, Sophia’s friend said, “No!” An incident report shows Sophia’s eyes were “swollen shut.” Medics rushed her to the hospital by ambulance. She spent time in intensive care for a severe food allergy, but recovered. “It was pretty scary,” Sophia said. Next, Sophia said she braced for her bills. “I have insurance through my husband’s work,” she explained. She expected a 20% co-pay. Maybe a couple hundred dollars. But then, a surprise ambulance bill. Sophia was on the hook for a $4,517 balance because her insurance company, Cigna, only covered $927 of the $5,444 the ambulance company charged. “I was shocked,” she said. “That’s a lot of money..” Sophia went digging and found AB 716. “We ended surprise ambulance bills in the state,” said Assemblymember Tasha Boerner, from Encinitas. She told NBC Bay Area that she heard from many constituents – like Sophia- who were caught between a health plan and an ambulance company over an emergency ambulance ride. “It’s really heartbreaking,” Boerner said. So, she sponsored AB 716 to stop surprise ambulance bills. It’s now state law. Since 2024, California law has basically told health plans and ambulance companies to work out their billing disputes themselves, and stop sending patients a bill for the balance. “It was such an obvious gap to close,” Boerner said. But, it turns out AB 716 doesn’t apply to Sophia and millions of others. Why? A surprise technicality. Sophia doesn’t actually have traditional health insurance. She’s part of a “self-funded health plan.” That means her husband’s employer pays claims in the background, while Cigna handles front end administration. “Self funded” plans are generally federally regulated, so state laws like AB 716 do not apply. “We just don’t have jurisdiction over the federal plans,” Boerner explained. If you work for a large company, your insurance card likely says “self funded.” An Employee Benefit Research Institute report estimates about 75% of companies with 500 or more workers have “self funded” health plans. Federal law has a “no surprises” act, too. But here’s another surprise: it does not cover ambulance bills. a Harvard law school publication recently called ambulance bills, “The Last Gap in the No Surprises Act.” “I really urge congress to close that gap,” Boerner said. AMR, Sophia’s ambulance company, told NBC Bay Area it “would welcome a change to the law requiring federally regulated health plans to pay the approved rate for emergency ambulance services.” With neither federal nor state protection, it looked like Sophia had to pay the big, $4,500 balance bill for her emergency ambulance ride. Then, one final surprise. NBC Bay Area asked Cigna about Sophia’s case. It said somewhere in the billing process Sophia’s lifesaving ride was charged wrong because in Santa Clara County, the county sets ambulance rates. Cigna said, “Thank you for bringing this to our attention. The claim has been reprocessed in accordance with county-established ambulance rates.” Sophia said her $4,500 bill then dropped to just $300. “Thank you for all your help. I really appreciate it,” she said. “I really felt like I wasn’t getting anywhere on my own. I felt like I was getting the runaround.” When you have health plan problems, government regulators can help you file an official complaint. The state covers traditional health insurance with the Department of Managed Health Care. If your health plan is “self funded,” you can turn to the federal government’s Employee Benefits Security Administration. To know which plan you have, look at your insurance card or talk to your employer’s personnel department.

headlines.title: San Jose mayor meets with neighbors complaining about data center noise
headlines.description: On Wednesday night, Mayor Matt Mahan met with some South San Jose residents who say they’ve been dealing with a low, constant hum and bright lights shinning into their backyards coming from data centers nearby. Neighbors said the noise can get even louder when temperatures rise. Their concerns come as San Jose looks at whether its rules for data centers need to be strengthened. Denisa and Jay Filichia live in South San Jose. Their backyard faces several data centers along Great Oaks Boulevard, separated by a few roads and train tracks. “We’re not anti-data center at all, it’s more the noise and the lights that are bothering us,” Filichia said. Denisa has been in contact with the city, and on Wednesday night, Mayor Matt Mahan went to the neighborhood to hear the noise for himself. The mayor and the neighbors then walked toward Monterey Road, getting closer to the data centers. The neighbors’ complaints come as data centers themselves are facing increased scrutiny in other cities as these facilities usually require significant amounts of electricity and water, causing a lot of anger in some communities. Some are even imposing temporary moratoriums on new data centers, all together. San Jose hasn’t. The city is hearing from residents and considering stronger standards. “We should require that if a data center in San Jose can access our purple pipe, that’s our recycled water network, that they need to hook up to that system and become a customer and pay for that water,” Mahan said. Mahan says that would also help the city expand its recycled water system. And for Denisa and Jay, he says he’ll work with the data centers to try to address the noise and light. “We’ll talk to them. Maybe they can put some insulation or shielding around the fans and quiet down on their end. maybe we can turn down the lights,” Mahan said. San Jose plans to hold a series of town halls in the coming months as it works on potential new standards and regulations for those data centers. As for any proposed rules they come up with, they’re expected to come before the San Jose City Council in December.
